location: Picasso, Miro, Dali: Unbound exhibition at MFA, Boston, MA

rows.stop: Le Lézard aux plumes d’or (The Lizard with Golden Feathers)
rows.text: Joan Miró's Le Lézard aux plumes d’or is an illustrated book with 40 color lithographs, bound in publisher's vellum. Louis Broder, a French publisher of illustrated books, commissioned Miró in 1971 to revive the tradition of the illustrated book. Miró's vibrant imagery was faithfully reproduced, capturing the essence of the natural and fantastical. The collaboration between Miró, Broder, and exemplifies the book's integration of text, image, and typography. Boris Fridman, a contributor to the art community, later donated this set to the Museum of Fine Arts, Boston, enriching its collection with an example of artistic innovation through collaboration.
rows.orientation: You are about to explore the Picasso, Miro, Dali: Unbound exhibition at the Museum of Fine Arts in Boston. This exhibition showcases the transformative power of the livre d'artiste, revolutionizing the book as an art form through deeply collaborative ventures rarely on view, exploring the intersection of images, words, and typography in Gallery 184. Within this exploration of human understanding and expression, you will encounter three extraordinary works by Spanish artists: Le Lézard aux plumes d’or (The Lizard with Golden Feathers), Au Soleil du Plafond, and Moses and Monotheism. rows.text: The work captures the essence of their partnership, merging Gris's geometric visual language with Reverdy's evocative prose. Their collaboration exemplifies the exhibition's thesis that the book can serve as a unified art form, integrating image, text, and typography into a single artistic expression. The significance of this work lies not only in its visual and literary synthesis but also in its historical context. Gris's untimely death in 1927 left the project unfinished, only to be completed posthumously in 1955. Reverdy's contribution further enriches the narrative, as his text weaves seamlessly with Gris's lithographs, turning the pages into a symphony of visual poetry.This work's presence in the MFA's exhibit offers a unique opportunity to witness the intersection of literature and visual art, inviting reflection on how light, both literal and metaphorical, guides us to deeper truths.
rows.orientation: Look for Au Soleil du Plafond in the galleries.

rows.text:
In 1974, Salvador Dalí crafted ten drypoints and lithographs on sheepskin as a response to Sigmund Freud’s last publication, "Moses and Monotheism." Freud, the pioneering psychoanalyst, authored this provocative text that reimagines Moses as an Egyptian nobleman, challenging traditional narratives. Dalí's illustrations enhance this text, offering a surrealistic interpretation that aligns with Freud’s radical theories. The decision to create this work in a limited edition of ten copies highlights the exclusivity and significance of the collaboration. Published by The Hogarth Press, this set embodies the exhibition’s thesis that artist-author collaborations revolutionized the book form, treating it as a comprehensive artwork. This legacy is echoed throughout the exhibition, inviting reflection on transformative ideas that continue to resonate today, much like Boston’s historic revolutionary spirit.

That's 3 stops — Au Soleil du Plafond, Gris's death in 1927 halted the project until 1955 and Moses and Monotheism, The Hogarth Press published this revolutionary artist-author collaboration.
